title: 7 best day trips from Dublin
summary: Discover the 7 best day trips from Dublin, with travel times, what to see, and costs, plus the easy way to pay in euros on the day. Compare.
body_markdown:
Some of my favourite memories of Ireland involve no big plans, just a train ticket, a seaside town and probably a little rain. When Dún Laoghaire became my home in Ireland, weekend plans often meant hopping on the DART and discovering somewhere new along the coast.


I spent two years getting to know the area, and there's so much more to explore beyond Dublin's city centre. Here are seven day trips I'd recommend, with a few local tips and practical details to help you plan yours.


The best day trips from Dublin include Howth, Dún Laoghaire and Dalkey, Glendalough, Bray, Malahide, Kilkenny and Powerscourt Estate. Most are within an hour of Dublin by train or car, while Glendalough and Kilkenny take a little longer. Coastal trips can cost as little as €4 return with a Leap Card, and many of the best things to do are free.


## Best day trips from Dublin: Travel times and costs


One of the things I loved about living near Dublin was how easy it was to explore without a car. You could take the DART along the coast, spend an afternoon in a small village or head into the countryside for something completely different.


Here's how the seven destinations compare.

## 1. Howth: The perfect coastal escape from Dublin


Alejandro Luengo/Unsplash


Howth is one of those places where you can arrive without much of a plan and still have a fantastic day. It's a working fishing village with colourful boats, seafood restaurants and beautiful coastal trails, all about half an hour from Dublin.


Start with a walk around the harbour. Keep an eye on the water because seals sometimes appear near the fishing boats, especially when there's activity around the harbour.


From there, head towards the East Pier and lighthouse. If you're up for a longer walk, follow one of the Howth Cliff Walk routes for views of Dublin Bay, Ireland's Eye and the Irish Sea.


One of the nicest things about Howth is the atmosphere. There's always something happening around the harbour, from fishermen unloading their catch to people queuing for fish and chips.


**A little local tip:** Don't feel you have to do the longest cliff walk. The harbour and pier are lovely on their own, especially if the weather is unpredictable. And if you want to eat seafood, try arriving before the lunchtime rush on weekends.


**How to get there:** Take the DART from Dublin Connolly or another central station directly to Howth.


**Travel time:** Around 25-35 minutes each way.


**Estimated cost:** Around €4 return with an adult Leap Card. The harbour and cliff walks are free.


## 2. Dún Laoghaire, Dalkey and Killiney: A little piece of home


I couldn't write about day trips from Dublin without including Dún Laoghaire. It was home for much of my time in Ireland, and I still miss the walks along the East Pier, the little cafés and those days when the sea looked beautiful even under a completely grey sky.


Start with the East Pier, one of the town's most popular walking spots. It's a simple pleasure, but that's exactly what makes it special. Afterwards, stop at Teddy's for an ice cream, something of a local tradition.


If you're curious about Irish sea-swimming culture, walk towards Sandycove and the Forty Foot. People swim there throughout the year, including in winter. You don't have to join them to appreciate the experience!


Then take the DART a little further south to Dalkey. This small village has charming streets, independent shops, old pubs and a medieval castle.


For the best views, continue towards Killiney Hill. On a clear day, you can see Dublin Bay, the Wicklow Mountains and the coastline stretching into the distance.


**A little local tip:** When travelling south from central Dublin, try sitting on the left-hand side of the DART. The sea views are part of the experience, particularly around Blackrock, Dún Laoghaire and Dalkey. Also, don't try to rush all three places. I'd spend more time in Dún Laoghaire and Dalkey, adding Killiney Hill if the weather is good.


**How to get there:** Take the southbound DART from Dublin city centre. Dún Laoghaire, Dalkey and Killiney are stops along the same line.


**Travel time:** Around 20-45 minutes, depending on your destination.


**Estimated cost:** Around €4-€6 with an adult Leap Card, depending on the number of journeys. The East Pier, Forty Foot and Killiney Hill are free.


## 3. Glendalough: Ancient history in the Wicklow Mountains


**Hamed Alayoub/Unsplash**


If you want to see a different side of Ireland, head to Glendalough in County Wicklow.


The name means *valley of the two lakes* , and the landscape is exactly what you'd imagine: mountains, forests, quiet walking trails and two beautiful glacial lakes.


But Glendalough is more than a nature destination. It's also home to an early medieval monastic settlement associated with St Kevin, including an impressive round tower, stone churches and an old cemetery.


I'd start by exploring the monastic ruins before walking towards the Upper Lake. The route is relatively easy, and the scenery gets more dramatic as you move further into the valley.


If you're a keen hiker, there are longer routes through the surrounding hills. Just remember that some involve steep climbs and exposed terrain.


**A little local tip:** Many visitors head straight for the lakes and spend very little time around the monastic settlement. Don't skip it. The history adds another dimension to the visit, especially when you realise how long people have been coming to this valley.


**How to get there:** Take St Kevin's Bus from Dublin, or drive through County Wicklow.


**Travel time:** Around 1.5-2 hours by bus.


**Estimated cost:** €23 return by St Kevin's Bus. Walking around the lakes and monastic ruins is free, while the visitor centre and parking may involve additional charges.


Check the return bus timetable before starting a long walk.


## 4. Bray: A proper Irish seaside afternoon


Bray has a completely different atmosphere from Howth or Dalkey. It's a traditional seaside town with a long promenade, amusement attractions, cafés and a beach that fills with people whenever the sun appears.


I love the idea of a classic Irish seaside day: a walk along the promenade, something to eat and a little time just watching the sea.


If you're feeling energetic, climb Bray Head. It's a fairly short but steep walk, and the views from the top are worth the effort. You'll see the Irish Sea, the coastline and the Wicklow Mountains.


Bray is also a good destination if you're travelling with friends or family and don't want to organise too much. You can spend a few hours walking, eating and exploring without needing tickets or reservations.


**A little local tip:** Older travel guides often recommend the Bray to Greystones Cliff Walk, but the through route remains closed because of landslide risks. Instead, choose one of the officially open Bray Head walking routes. You can still enjoy beautiful coastal views without attempting the closed trail.


**How to get there:** Take the southbound DART from Dublin.


**Travel time:** Around 40-50 minutes each way.


**Estimated cost:** Around €4 return with an adult Leap Card. The promenade and Bray Head walking routes are free.


## 5. Malahide: Castle grounds, cafés and a charming village


**Barbara McDermott/Unsplash**


Malahide is one of the easiest day trips from Dublin, but it often gets overlooked in favour of the more famous coastal towns.


Its main attraction is Malahide Castle, which has a history stretching back centuries. The castle is surrounded by extensive parkland, beautiful gardens and walking paths.


You can book a guided tour to explore the interiors and learn about the Talbot family, who lived there for generations.


But I'd also make time for Malahide village itself. There are lovely cafés, independent shops, restaurants and a marina, making it a great place for a relaxed afternoon.


One of the best ways to enjoy Malahide is to combine a walk through the castle grounds with lunch in the village, then continue towards the waterfront if the weather cooperates.


**A little local tip:** You don't have to pay for a castle tour to enjoy Malahide. Much of the surrounding parkland is free to explore. If you're travelling on a budget, bring something for a picnic and spend your afternoon outdoors.


**How to get there:** Take the DART from Dublin Connolly to Malahide.


**Travel time:** Around 25-35 minutes each way.


**Estimated cost:** Around €4 return with an adult Leap Card. Castle admission is approximately €17 per adult, subject to the ticket option and current pricing.


## 6. Kilkenny: Medieval streets and traditional Irish pubs


**NIR HIMI/Unsplash**


Kilkenny is a little further away, but it's one of the best options if you're interested in Irish history and want to explore somewhere that feels different from Dublin.


The city is famous for its medieval architecture, narrow streets, traditional pubs and impressive castle overlooking the River Nore.


Start at Kilkenny Castle and walk through its grounds before exploring the Medieval Mile, which connects some of the city's most important historic sites.


Along the way, you'll find old stone buildings, independent shops, cafés and small lanes that are worth exploring without a map.


Kilkenny also has a strong arts and crafts tradition. If you enjoy browsing local shops, look out for Irish ceramics, jewellery and textiles.


**A little local tip:** Don't spend your entire visit moving between paid attractions. Kilkenny is one of those places where simply wandering through the streets is part of the experience. And if you enjoy traditional pubs, it's worth stopping for lunch or an early drink before returning to Dublin.


**How to get there:** Take the train from Dublin Heuston to Kilkenny MacDonagh Station.


**Travel time:** Around 1 hour 30 minutes to 1 hour 45 minutes each way.


**Estimated cost:** Advance online train tickets can start from around €9.99 each way, meaning a return journey may cost approximately €20 when the lowest fares are available. Prices rise depending on the service and booking date.


Check[Irish Rail's web fares](https://www.irishrail.ie/en-ie/offer/webfares) before booking, as buying in advance is usually the best way to find lower prices.


## 7. Powerscourt Estate and Enniskerry: Gardens with a mountain backdrop


**Manuel Hiller/Pixabay**


If you're looking for beautiful scenery without committing to a long hike, Powerscourt Estate is a lovely option.


Located in County Wicklow, just outside Enniskerry village, the estate is known for its landscaped gardens and views of the Great Sugar Loaf mountain.


The gardens include formal terraces, ornamental lakes, woodland paths and Japanese-inspired areas. It's the kind of place where you can spend hours wandering around, especially in spring and summer.


Afterwards, head into Enniskerry, a small village with a picturesque square, cafés and traditional buildings.


One thing worth knowing is that Powerscourt Gardens and Powerscourt Waterfall are separate attractions. The waterfall is several kilometres from the main estate, so visiting both is easier if you have a car.


**A little local tip:** If you're relying on public transport, I'd focus on the gardens and Enniskerry village rather than trying to fit in the waterfall. The gardens alone are worth the trip, and you'll have more time to enjoy them.


**How to get there:** Drive from Dublin or take public transport towards Enniskerry, checking local bus connections and walking distances in advance.


**Travel time:** Around 45-60 minutes by car, or longer by public transport.


**Estimated cost:** Powerscourt Gardens admission is approximately €14 per adult. Public transport costs vary depending on your route and connections. The waterfall requires a separate ticket, approximately €8 per adult.


## Which day trips from Dublin are best without a car?


One of the biggest advantages of staying in Dublin is that you don't need to rent a car to explore some beautiful places nearby.


For coastal destinations, the DART is usually your best option. It connects Dublin with Howth, Malahide, Dún Laoghaire, Dalkey, Killiney and Bray.


And the train journey itself can be lovely, particularly along the southern coastline.


If you're travelling without a car, I'd prioritise Howth, Dún Laoghaire and Dalkey, Bray or Malahide. They're easy to reach, affordable and give you plenty to do without organising additional transport.


Kilkenny is also accessible by direct train, while Glendalough has a dedicated bus service.


Powerscourt requires a little more planning because public transport connections are less convenient.


### How much does public transport cost around Dublin?


The TFI Leap Card is worth considering if you're planning several day trips.


For eligible adult journeys within Dublin's Zone 1, the TFI 90 Minute fare costs €2. There's also a €6 daily cap, so you can make multiple qualifying journeys without spending more than that amount in one day.


That makes visiting several coastal towns surprisingly affordable.


For longer journeys, such as Kilkenny, check Irish Rail's advance fares. Booking early can make a noticeable difference to the price.


You can use[Transport for Ireland](https://www.transportforireland.ie/) to plan local journeys and compare routes.


## What about Galway, Belfast and the Cliffs of Moher?


**Evgeni Gitlits/Unsplash**


You might have noticed that some of Ireland's most famous destinations aren't on this list.


That's intentional.


Galway, Belfast, the Cliffs of Moher and the Giant's Causeway are all popular excursions from Dublin, but I think they deserve more time than a rushed day trip.


The Cliffs of Moher, for example, are around 3.5-4 hours from Dublin by road. That's a lot of travelling for a few hours of sightseeing.


Galway and Belfast are closer, but both have enough to explore to justify staying overnight.


If you have only a few days in Dublin, I'd recommend exploring the surrounding coast or County Wicklow instead. You'll spend less time travelling and more time actually enjoying the places you visit.


And if you're planning a longer European trip, you might also enjoy our guide to the[best day trips from London](https://grey.co/blog/best-day-trips-from-london) , with more ideas for exploring beyond a capital city.


## Tips for planning day trips from Dublin


A few things I learnt during my time in Ireland can make these little adventures much more enjoyable.


**Don't wait for perfect weather.** If you do, you might spend your entire trip indoors! Bring a waterproof jacket, wear comfortable shoes and be prepared for the weather to change throughout the day.


**Use the DART whenever possible.** It's convenient, affordable and offers beautiful coastal views. You also avoid worrying about parking.


**Leave room for spontaneous stops.** Sometimes the best part of a day trip is finding a lovely café, a quiet beach or a little street you hadn't planned to visit.


**Check transport schedules in advance.** This is particularly important for Glendalough and Powerscourt, where public transport is less frequent.


**Avoid trying to see too much.** I'd rather spend a relaxed afternoon exploring one or two places than rush through five attractions just to tick them off a list.

## Frequently asked questions about day trips from Dublin


### What is the best day trip from Dublin?


Howth is one of the best options because it's only around 30 minutes from Dublin by DART and offers coastal walks, seafood restaurants and beautiful views. For a quieter seaside experience, Dún Laoghaire and Dalkey are also excellent choices.


### What is the cheapest day trip from Dublin?


Howth, Bray, Malahide and Dún Laoghaire are among the cheapest options. Return DART journeys can cost around €4 with an adult Leap Card, and many outdoor attractions are free.


### Can you visit the Cliffs of Moher on a day trip from Dublin?


Yes, but it's a long journey. The drive takes approximately 3.5–4 hours each way, and organised tours can last 12–14 hours. If possible, consider staying overnight in Galway or County Clare.


### What are the best day trips from Dublin by train?


Howth, Dún Laoghaire, Dalkey, Killiney, Bray and Malahide are all accessible by DART. Kilkenny is another good option, with direct trains from Dublin Heuston taking around 1.5 hours.


### Is Glendalough worth visiting from Dublin?


Yes. Glendalough is a beautiful destination for hiking, nature and history. Its two lakes and medieval monastic ruins make it one of the most interesting places to visit in County Wicklow.


### Can you visit Dún Laoghaire, Dalkey and Killiney in one day?


Absolutely. They're all located along the same DART line, making them easy to combine. You can walk along the East Pier in Dún Laoghaire, explore Dalkey village and finish with views from Killiney Hill.


### Do you need a car for day trips from Dublin?


Not necessarily. Many of the best destinations are accessible by DART or train, including Howth, Bray, Malahide and Kilkenny. A car can be useful for more remote places in County Wicklow, but it's not essential for most coastal day trips.


## There's more to Dublin than the city itself


Dublin has plenty to offer, but some of the things I remember most fondly from my time in Ireland happened outside the city centre.


The little coastal towns, the walks along the sea, the cafés and those DART journeys with views that never seemed to get old.


So if you're visiting Dublin, leave at least one day free to explore beyond the city. You might find that your favourite memory of Ireland comes from somewhere you hadn't even planned to visit.
